subtype: Approach: catastrophising and self-blame [Pitfall]
passage:
In Lunglei, the Class 10 half-yearly results were pinned outside the headmaster's office, and Lalremsiami's name had a red mark beside mathematics: 28 out of 100.

She walked home the long way, past the church, thinking the same sentence over and over. That's it. No science stream. No nursing college. Nothing.

At home she pushed her maths books under the bed. For the next two weeks she didn't open them. When her classmate Bhupen came by with notes from the extra class, she said, "What's the point? I've already failed my life."

"It was one exam," Bhupen said. "The half-yearly doesn't even count for boards."

She didn't answer. She was so sure she was right that she never checked.

The pre-board came six weeks later. With two weeks lost, she scored 31. Barely better. The certainty had cost her the time to recover.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami score in the half-yearly mathematics exam?
qa.a: 28 out of 100.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she walked home the long way?
qa.a: She felt hopeless and crushed, convinced that one bad mark had ruined her whole future.

qa.q: What would have helped more than pushing the books away?
qa.a: Checking the facts, like Bhupen's point that the half-yearly does not count for boards, and making a small recovery plan with a teacher.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt when she said she had failed her life?
qa.a: Bhupen was probably worried and a bit helpless, trying to give her facts that she was not ready to hear.

grounding: Shows a student concluding that one failure means a ruined future and stopping study, a certainty that skips the evidence and makes recovery harder.

subtype: Approach: catastrophising and self-blame [Pitfall]

Yuki had failed the first-term chemistry test at her high school in Sendai: 32 out of 100. On the train home, she thought, if I can't pass chemistry, I'll never get into a medical course. I'll never be anything.

By the time she got off at her station, it felt like fact.

For three weeks she stopped doing chemistry homework. What's the point, she told herself. Her older brother, Hiroshi, noticed the untouched workbook on her desk. "Didn't you say one test is only fifteen percent of the term grade?"

"It doesn't matter. I'm just bad at it."

"Did your teacher say that?"

She hadn't asked. She hadn't checked anything. She'd just been sure.

The second test came. She scored 35. The first failure hadn't ruined her future, but three weeks of giving up had made the next test harder.

qa.q: What did Yuki score on the first-term chemistry test?

qa.a: She felt despairing and panicked, as if her whole future had collapsed.

subtype: Approach: telling parents and asking for support [Action]

Last March I failed my Class 11 physics final. I'm Aparna, and I remember sitting on the school steps with the result, hands cold, thinking my parents would be furious.

I wanted to hide it. But I knew hiding it would be worse later. So I spent that evening writing something first: a page called "What I'll do". Supplementary exam in July. Two doubt sessions a week with Lalit Sir. A timetable for the holidays.

At dinner I put the result and the page on the table. My father's face went tight. My mother said, "How could this happen?" in that voice. For a few minutes it was bad.

Then my father picked up the page and read it twice. "Okay," he said. "We'll pay for the supplementary form tomorrow. I'll call Lalit Sir myself."

I passed in July. But mostly I remember not having to carry it alone.

qa.q: When was the supplementary exam?
qa.a: In July.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel sitting on the school steps with the result?
qa.a: Aparna felt frightened and anxious, hands cold, expecting the parents to be furious.

qa.a: Bringing a written recovery plan helped the parents move from anger to action; Aparna could also ask them to check in weekly on the timetable.

Class teacher's note, Class 12 Commerce, after the pre-board results

Afreen stayed back after the bell on Thursday. She had failed accountancy and was sure her parents would be angry. She asked if she could just not tell them until the finals.

I told her that would leave them no chance to help. We spent twenty minutes on a single page instead: the marks, the topics she had lost, and a plan: supplementary practice papers, and two extra doubt sessions a week with me.

On Monday her mother, Mrs. Jaya Qureshi, came to see me. She admitted the first evening had been tense, with raised voices. But by the next morning the family had read Afreen's page and agreed to it. She asked me to confirm the session times.

Afreen has attended both sessions this week. I will review her progress with her mother at the end of the month.

subtype: Approach: hiding the result [Pitfall]

The marksheet came on Friday, and the maths line said 22 out of 80. Aparna folded it into eighths and hid it inside her geography atlas. Her parents were away at a wedding in Jaipur till Tuesday. She had four days.

She told her cousin Deepak on the phone, "I'll fix it quietly. I'll pass the re-test and they'll never know."

But she didn't know when the re-test forms were due, and she couldn't ask the teacher without the teacher asking about her parents. Every night she lay awake thinking about the atlas on the shelf.

On Wednesday, her father found a school notice in her bag: re-test applications, last date Monday, parent's signature required. The date had passed two days ago.

He didn't shout. He just looked at her and said, "Why didn't you tell me?" That hurt more than shouting.

In their Pune housing society, Mridul was known as the boy who always topped. So when his Class 11 chemistry result came back as a fail, he put the report card in his school bag's inner pocket and told his parents the results were "delayed".

His best friend Madhav, from the next building, found out when they were walking to tuition. "You have to tell them."

"I'll just clear the re-exam first. Then I'll tell them it went fine."

At home, his mother held out her hand for the report card. Her voice was quiet. "Three weeks, Mridul. You lied to us for three weeks."

Two weeks later, a Saturday: Yusuf's list was pinned above his desk. First: the July supplementary. If that failed: open school for the two subjects. Also: look at the diploma. "It's not the same road," he told his mother, "but it still goes somewhere."

I'm Reena. After I failed it in Class 11, everybody had big plans for me. My uncle said, "Now you'll top the class." My mother printed a timetable for all six subjects. I tried it for three days and wanted to cry.

Then my mentor at the tuition centre, Mrs. Das, said something different. "Forget topping. Let's just clear chemistry first."

So we made a weekly plan only for chemistry. One chapter a week. Ten questions every evening. A small test every Saturday with her.

The first Saturday I got 12 out of 25. Then 15. Then 19. Honestly, getting 19 felt better than any topper fantasy. It made me believe I could do it.

When I cleared the re-test in October, I started adding physics. One subject at a time.

The next week he was back in bed by eleven, and he and Arif had a past-paper session on Sunday. I can't say what he felt. But he wasn't treating the fail like a verdict anymore.

The counsellor's room at the hill school in Darjeeling had a window facing the tea gardens. Dolma had walked past it for weeks without going in.

It had been two months since the board results. Everyone said she'd feel better soon. She didn't. She couldn't eat much. She had stopped playing basketball. She kept thinking nothing would ever get better.

Her friend Rashmi had noticed. That Tuesday, at lunch, Dolma said quietly, "Sometimes I feel like there's no point to anything." Rashmi didn't laugh it off. She put down her tiffin. "Come with me. Right now."

She walked Dolma to the counsellor's door and knocked. Ms. Lepcha looked up, saw Dolma's face, and cleared her afternoon. She listened, then called Dolma's parents while Dolma sat with her, and they arranged to meet together that evening.

Rashmi waited outside the whole hour.

Dear Jatin,

You asked why I disappeared for a few weeks after the results. I want to tell you honestly, because I think you're struggling too.

After I failed two subjects, I kept telling myself to just be stronger. Study harder, stop being sad. But it didn't lift. For almost a month I felt heavy every morning, like nothing I did would matter. I stopped answering messages, even yours.

One night I told my mother I didn't see the point of anything anymore. She didn't panic or scold. She sat with me, and that same night she called a helpline with me beside her. The next morning she took me to the school counsellor, who is now helping me with a proper plan, and we meet every week.

It wasn't about willpower. I needed people trained for this.

If you feel that way, please tell someone today.

Minakshi

Santiago was sixteen and in his last year at a public secondary school in Valparaíso when a flyer appeared on the notice board: "March Against Bus Fare Hike - Thursday!" His friend Hana was already going. "Come on, everyone's in."

Then the city transport office's statement: the fare was rising by a fixed amount for students. Then two news sites that usually disagreed with each other.

He noticed the flyer said the student pass was being "abolished". The official statement said only that the price was going up. The newspapers agreed with the statement.

He texted Hana. "Still considering it. But the flyer exaggerates. What are we actually asking for?"

Hana replied, "Good question. Let me ask the organisers."

In the junior college library, a crumpled pamphlet lay on Gautam's table: "Fee Hike = Injustice! March Monday!" Disha, from the student council, dropped into the chair opposite. "Are you coming?"

"Maybe. First I want to know what's actually going on." Gautam pulled three printouts from his bag. "This is the college notice. Fees up by a set amount next year, for new admissions only. This is the principal's statement. And these are two newspaper reports."

"And?"

"The pamphlet says 'for everyone'. The notice says new students only. One paper agrees with the notice. The other doesn't mention it."

passage:
I'm Ayesha. My brother Kamal is in Class 12, and when the older students at his school planned a sit-in about the closed sports ground, I watched him think about it for two days.

He didn't just say yes or no. That first evening I heard him on the balcony talking to himself, sort of. "What do I actually care about? Fairness. The juniors have nowhere to play." Then, quieter: "But a sit-in during exams week, with the gate blocked. Is that the best way to get the ground back?"

The next day he had a sheet of paper on his desk with three columns: sit-in, petition, student council meeting. Under each he'd written what it might change and what it might risk.

He chose the petition and the council meeting. He got two hundred signatures in a week. I don't know if he felt sure. But he looked calmer than when he'd started.

qa.q: What were the three columns on Kamal's sheet?
qa.a: Sit-in, petition and student council meeting.

qa.q: What might Kamal have been feeling as he talked to himself on the balcony?
qa.a: He seemed torn and thoughtful, caring about fairness for the juniors but uneasy about a sit-in during exams week.

qa.q: What else could Kamal do if the council meeting does not work?
qa.a: He could write to the principal with the petition attached, still using calm, lawful steps to push for the ground.

qa.q: How did Kamal's decision look to Ayesha?
qa.a: To Ayesha it looked careful and calm, weighing options on paper, though Ayesha admits not knowing whether he felt sure.

grounding: An observer describes a teen asking which principle matters most and whether a sit-in or a petition or council meeting would serve the cause better.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest

passage:
Monday: Farida's class chat group was full of plans for a rally against cutting the evening bus route. Her friend Deepika was going. Farida sat on her bed with a notebook and wrote one question at the top: "What do I actually care about here?" She wrote: fairness for kids from far villages who need that bus. And safety.

Wednesday: She added columns. Rally on a busy highway: loud, but risky, and her parents would worry. Petition to the transport office: slow, but safe. Letter from the school council: official, and the principal might sign it too.

Friday: She told Deepika, "I'm not skipping this. I'm choosing the part that might actually work." She took the petition to every class and got 312 signatures. Deepika came back from the rally tired. "Maybe we need both," she admitted.

qa.q: How many signatures did Farida get?
qa.a: 312 signatures.

qa.q: How did Farida feel as she worked through her columns?
qa.a: She felt thoughtful and torn, caring about fairness for village kids while worried about safety and her parents' concern.

qa.q: What else could Farida try to strengthen the petition?
qa.a: She could ask the principal to sign the council letter along with it, so the transport office hears from students and school together.

qa.q: How did Farida's choice look to Deepika by Friday?
qa.a: Deepika, tired after the rally, seemed to see value in Farida's approach, admitting they might need both.

grounding: Shows a teen asking which principle matters most and weighing whether a rally, a petition or a school council letter would serve that cause better.
